stories.headline: Trump Flies to Asia: ASEAN and Quad Meetings in Manila, Then a First Three-Way Talk With Xi and Putin in Shenzhen
stories.what_happened: On 16 November President Trump left for Asia. He arrives in Manila on 17 November for the ASEAN summit and a Quad meeting with India, Japan and Australia, then flies to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC summit, where on 19 November he is due to hold the first-ever three-way meeting with Xi Jinping and Vladimir Putin, focused on nuclear stockpiles. India's PM Modi is also in Manila for the ASEAN-India and East Asia summits.
stories.why_it_matters: The leaders of the world's biggest nuclear powers have not met together before; officials say this is a starting point, not a deal. The Manila meetings show how Asia's countries balance ties with the US and China.

key_facts.fact: US President Donald Trump left Joint Base Andrews, Maryland, on Monday 16 November 2026 for a trip to Asia.
Trump's first stop is Manila, the capital of the Philippines, for the 49th ASEAN Summit, held 15-17 November.
Trump arrives in Manila on Tuesday 17 November for the US-ASEAN Summit and related events.
ASEAN, the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, has 11 members; the Philippines is the 2026 chair.
The White House said Trump will sign a trade deal with Thailand while in Manila.
In Manila, Trump will meet Southeast Asian leaders who look to the US for help countering Beijing's aggression.

On Tuesday Trump is due to hold a Quad leaders' meeting with India, Japan and Australia on Indo-Pacific security; the White House says it is the first in-person Quad leaders' summit in two years and Trump's first in his current term.

The Quad meeting is expected to bring together Trump, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi, Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi and Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese; it is the group's first leaders-level meeting since September 2024.
On Wednesday Trump has a state visit and lunch with Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. at the presidential palace, then flies to Shenzhen, China, for the APEC summit.
APEC stands for Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation; its leaders' summit is in Shenzhen on 18 and 19 November.
On Thursday 19 November, after the APEC leaders' plenary, Trump is due to meet Chinese President Xi Jinping at Kylin Villa in Shenzhen, and Russian President Vladimir Putin is due to join them there.
The three-way meeting will be the first ever between the leaders of the US, China and Russia, and is to focus on nuclear stockpiles.
A White House official said no denuclearization agreement is expected; the session is a starting point for talks on shrinking nuclear stockpiles.

China's foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said on Monday the leaders would hold 'in-depth exchanges on safeguarding world peace and promoting strategic stability', and called the meeting of 'ground-breaking significance'.
China has long insisted that the US and Russia reduce their own large nuclear arsenals before it will agree to talks on its own stockpile.
The last nuclear arms treaty between the US and Russia expired in February 2026.
US officials had said on Friday that Trump would avoid Russia's war in Ukraine, but Trump said he will raise it with Xi and Putin.
Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has worried the leaders could use the summit to redraw spheres of influence, warning against a repeat of the 1945 Yalta Conference.
At the 1945 Yalta Conference, the leaders of the US, Britain and the Soviet Union agreed to divide Germany and Berlin into four military occupation zones and finalised plans for the United Nations.
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov dismissed the Yalta comparisons, noting any agreements reached in Shenzhen cannot be enforced on others.
Trump also wants to discuss the war in Iran with Xi and Putin.
Trump said North Korean leader Kim Jong Un 'may come' to Shenzhen, but that 'that's up to President Xi.'
Trump met Kim three times in his first term.

A 2025 meeting between Trump and Xi in Busan, South Korea, produced a trade truce that cut some US tariffs on Chinese goods in exchange for looser Chinese limits on rare earth exports; the truce expires in January.
This is Trump's second trip to China this year; tech executive Elon Musk is travelling with him.
Trump's last face-to-face meeting with Putin was in Alaska in August 2025.
Trump's Republican Party lost both chambers of Congress in the November midterm elections.
Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi arrived in Manila on Monday 16 November for a two-day visit to attend the 23rd ASEAN-India Summit and the 21st East Asia Summit.
East Asia Summit members include the ASEAN states, India, China, Japan, South Korea, Australia, New Zealand, the US and Russia.

stories.headline: EU Sanctions Nearly 50 Russian Banks, Approves Its Largest Payment to Ukraine and Says a Ceasefire Must Come First
stories.what_happened: On 16 November EU foreign ministers in Brussels added 113 new names to their sanctions on Russia, including nearly 50 banks and financial institutions, and EU ministers approved a payment of nearly 8 billion euros to Ukraine, the largest single payment under the Ukraine Facility. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas accused Russia of making demands to keep the war going and said a ceasefire must come first.
stories.why_it_matters: Sanctions and money are Europe's main tools in the war; the EU wants a say in peace talks led by the US and is using them as leverage.

key_facts.fact: EU foreign ministers met in Brussels on Monday 16 November at the Foreign Affairs Council, chaired by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas.
The new sanctions list 12 individuals and 101 entities, 113 in total, including nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions.
The EU Council said: 'The EU is cutting off the financial channels that process state revenues and fund Russia's war effort.'

Also listed are the sole shareholder of Russian online retailer Wildberries, a majority owner of Ozon, companies running Russian refineries and the St Petersburg oil terminal, and firms in the UAE, China, Seychelles and Oman that buy Russian oil products.
People and companies on the list have their assets frozen; EU operators may not give them money or economic resources; the 12 individuals also face EU travel bans.
Dozens of people accused of spreading pro-Russian propaganda and disinformation were also hit with travel bans and asset freezes.
Kallas said Russia was repeating demands made before its full-scale invasion and adding conditions, calling this 'a clear pretext for keeping the war going.'
Kallas wrote on X: 'In 2021, Russia's demands were a pretext for war. In 2026, they are pretext to keep the war going.'
Kallas wrote that 'A ceasefire must come first.'
Kallas said: 'We have leverage. That is our sanctions. That is frozen assets.'
The EU approved a payment of nearly 8 billion euros (about $8.7bn) to Ukraine, its largest-ever single payment under the Ukraine Facility.
Around 5 billion euros of the payment comes from 2026 resources of the Ukraine Support Loan, and the Council says Kyiv completed more than 20 reform steps to unlock it.
The Ukraine Facility dates from March 2024 and offers more than 50 billion euros in grants and loans through 2027; once these funds arrive, total payments since mid-2024 will pass 40 billion euros.
Kyiv also received $1.88bn from the European Commission to buy drones, ammunition and air defence systems, part of a $99bn loan approved in February.
Two days of US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks in the UAE produced a prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on ending the war.
After the Abu Dhabi talks, the US encouraged Ukraine and its backers to accept a Russian demand for a new European security framework; Europeans see this as an attempt to weaken NATO.

Five countries - the UK, France, Germany, Italy and Poland - plus officials from the European Council and NATO will speak on Europe's behalf in any future peace talks, leaders agreed after a meeting in Dublin.
Russian attacks killed at least three people in Ukraine on Monday, in the Kherson, Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhia regions.
Russia's Defence Ministry said it intercepted 1,336 Ukrainian drones overnight.
EU humanitarian chief Hadja Lahbib said Russia is 'turning winter into a weapon of war' as she unveiled a new aid package for Ukraine.
The EU is pushing for a ceasefire followed by a lasting peace agreement; the war is in its fifth year.

stories.headline: COP31 Enters Its Final Week With a First Draft Deal and Deep Divisions
stories.what_happened: The UN climate summit in Antalya, Türkiye, began its second week on 16 November with an 18-page first draft of its main 'cover decision', including a target for electricity to supply 35% of world energy by 2035 and $120 billion a year in adaptation money by 2035. Oil producers and large developing countries pushed back, and ministers arrive mid-week to bargain.
stories.why_it_matters: The cover decision is the summit's main statement of what countries will do next on climate change; it needs every country's agreement.

key_facts.fact: The second week of the UN climate conference COP31 in Antalya, Türkiye, opened on 16 November with a pessimistic outlook.
An 18-page first draft of the cover decision was published on Monday 16 November; the Turkish presidency plans to bring ministers together mid-week to hear their views.
The draft tries to include all options from 45 submissions representing more than 160 governments.

The draft includes a 35x35 global electrification target, a carbon capture and storage goal, a call for developed countries to reach net zero by 2030, and $120 billion a year in adaptation finance by 2035.
Türkiye's voluntary pledge is to raise electricity to 35% of global final energy consumption by 2035.

The Arab Group and Like-Minded Developing Countries, which include major emerging economies, opposed new sector targets in the cover decision; Saudi Arabia rejected referencing Brazil's roadmap for moving away from fossil fuels.
India opposed mentioning scientific reports from outside the UN process, including a UN Environment Programme report on handling an overshoot of 1.5C.

Chris Bowen of Australia, the COP's President of Negotiations, said he published the draft earlier than previous presidencies, included measures his own country opposes, and that the final text will differ substantially.
Decisions at COP are made by consensus under UNFCCC rules, which Bowen said will be tested in the closing plenary.
Developing countries want the pledge to triple adaptation finance defined as at least $120 billion a year by 2035; donors have been reluctant to commit to specifics.

Germany's Heike Henn said the fossil fuel roadmap and electrification goal do not need to appear in the cover decision, and that the next Global Stocktake, due in 2028, is the right place for new number goals.
Ministers expected in Antalya include Bhupender Yadav (India), Wopke Hoekstra (EU), Miatta Fahnbulleh (UK) and Carsten Schneider (Germany).
An 18-member group of Democratic members of the US House arrived to say they will push climate action despite the absence of the US government.
Canada will loan up to C$560 million (US$392 million) over four years to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility, a fund to protect tropical forests; total pledges to it are about $8.2 billion.

Somalia, Uganda and Sierra Leone endorsed the Turkish presidency's voluntary pledge on sustainable AI, which covers low-emission data centres and efficient cooling, energy and water; nine countries and more than 40 companies have signed.

stories.headline: ASEAN and China Miss Their Goal of a South China Sea Code of Conduct
stories.what_happened: At the ASEAN summit in Manila, ASEAN and China failed to finish a code of conduct for the South China Sea, though about 80% of a draft was tentatively agreed. Whether the code would be legally binding is still unresolved, and Singapore takes over the task as chair next year.
stories.why_it_matters: The South China Sea is claimed in large part by China, overlapping with the waters of five Southeast Asian countries, and clashes at sea between China and the Philippines have raised tensions.

key_facts.fact: China and ASEAN failed to conclude long-running talks on a code of conduct for the South China Sea at meetings in Manila, even though about 80 percent of a draft was tentatively agreed.
Philippine Foreign Minister Theresa Lazaro told reporters on Sunday: 'There is no conclusion yet.'
Unresolved issues include whether the code would be legally binding.
ASEAN and Beijing have negotiated the code for more than two decades; the Philippines had pledged to reach a deal by the end of 2026.
Singapore becomes ASEAN chair next year, and Lazaro hopes the code can be concluded under Singapore's leadership.
China claims most of the South China Sea, overlapping with the exclusive economic zones of Brunei, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines and Vietnam.
A 2016 international arbitration tribunal ruled that China's sweeping claims have no basis under international law; Beijing rejects the ruling.

The Philippines accuses Chinese ships of aggressive acts in its waters, including water cannon firing and disrupting resupply missions; China accuses the Philippines of intruding on its territory. Beijing says its actions have been lawful and professional.
Southeast Asian nations want the code to reflect international law.
Philippine President Ferdinand Marcos Jr. opened the ASEAN summit's main meeting (the plenary) on 15 November.

ASEAN extended its ban on Myanmar's leader attending the bloc's summits, saying Myanmar had failed to follow a 2021 peace plan; Myanmar was due to chair ASEAN this year, but the role passed to the Philippines.

stories.headline: Estonia Will Close Its Border Crossings With Russia After a Foiled Attack on a Drone Factory
stories.what_happened: Estonia says it will close all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December after stopping what it calls an arson attempt ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence on a drone factory near Tallinn. Eight people living in Latvia were arrested. Russia says it will check whether the plan is real and called it Russophobia.
stories.why_it_matters: The crossings are among the few overland links between Russia and the EU still open, and European countries say Russia's 'hybrid' attacks are spreading beyond Ukraine.

key_facts.fact: Estonia said on Sunday 15 November it would close its border with Russia after stopping what it called an attempted arson attack on a drone factory ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence.
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna wrote: 'Estonia will close all Estonian-Russian border crossing points as of 1 December.'
The target was Threod Systems, an Estonian defence company in Viimsi, north of Tallinn, which makes reconnaissance and attack drones.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the GRU ordered a 'sabotage attempt' on Saturday night; heightened security and a quick police response averted extensive damage and the attackers were detained.
Chief prosecutor Astrid Asi said security forces arrested eight people living in Latvia.
Michal described the incident as part of Russia's wider 'hybrid war' against Europe and said Estonia 'will not be intimidated.'
Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Moscow would check whether Estonia planned to shut all crossings and, if so, would see it as more aggressive Russophobia.
In August, Milrem Robotics, a defence subcontractor in Tallinn, was targeted in an attempted arson attack, and Latvian nationals were arrested.
Estonia, an EU and NATO member, has three crossings with Russia: Narva in the north, and Luhamaa and Koidula in the south.
Russia suspended vehicle traffic through Narva in February 2024, but people on foot can still cross.
These crossings are among the few overland links between Russia and the EU still operating since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Tsahkna said he had told the Finnish, Latvian and Lithuanian foreign ministers about the decision.
Romania said drones struck three ships near the Sulina Canal, which links the Danube to the Black Sea, on Sunday 15 November; no one was hurt and crews put out fires.
Romania's Foreign Minister Dan Neculaescu said: 'We have had four alerts in 24 hours, and we have had three ships hit over the weekend. This is unacceptable.'
Sweden's Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard said increased hybrid warfare reflects the Kremlin's frustration that it is not winning in Ukraine; Sweden has spent much more on civil defence.

stories.headline: After a Faulty Router Grounded US Flights, Air Travel Returns to Normal
stories.what_happened: On Friday 13 November the FAA stopped all departing flights across the US for more than four hours after its communications network became unstable. Officials traced the problem to a router being replaced at a remote facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, which flooded older equipment with data. By Monday 16 November flights were close to normal, and the government is asking Congress for more money to modernise the system.
stories.why_it_matters: Air traffic control relies on an aging network; the outage stranded thousands of travellers and shows why the system is being upgraded.

key_facts.fact: The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop at 3:36 p.m. ET on Friday 13 November, while about 3,500 flights were in the air; all of those planes landed safely.
The ground stop was lifted around 8:20 p.m. ET Friday and lasted more than four hours.
It was the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when an FAA computer system malfunctioned; the one before followed the 11 September 2001 attacks.
On Friday about 9,159 flights were cancelled and 7,190 delayed, according to FlightAware.
FAA chief Bryan Bedford said 50,000 flights were scheduled Friday and 30,000 had been completed when the stop began.

On Sunday more than 2,300 US flights were cancelled and more than 10,400 delayed, though not all delays came from the ground stop; by 6:30 a.m. ET Monday about 250 Monday flights had been cancelled and 850 delayed.
Operations were slowly returning to normal or close to it at most major airlines on Monday 16 November.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a contractor from L3Harris, working at a remote FAA site, was switching old copper wire to fiber and replacing a router.
The new router began flooding other routers and overloaded the system, with about 1,000 log-on attempts every four to five seconds.
The FAA traced the problem to a router upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas; a similar upgrade at a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, weeks earlier compounded it.
Communications disruptions hit 17 of the FAA's 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers.

L3Harris, a defence contractor, owns and operates the telecommunications network that connects America's air traffic control system; the network is linked by thousands of aging industrial routers being replaced with new models.
Bedford said about 70% of the system has been moved from copper to fiber, and that the ground stop was issued 'out of an abundance of caution.'
Officials said there was no sign of a cyberattack; Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there were no indications of one.

Duffy said the FAA's modernisation is funded by a $12.5 billion down payment, which he said is not enough; the Trump administration raised its air traffic control funding request to $30 billion late Friday.
Two members of Congress, Rick Larsen and Andre Carson, said only $1 billion of the $12.5 billion approved by Congress has been used.
Officials said it is safe to fly; Duffy advised travellers to check with their airlines before going to the airport.

stories.headline: Van Hollen Says He Can Beat Schumer in a Secret Vote to Lead Senate Democrats
stories.what_happened: Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who is challenging Chuck Schumer to lead the Democrats in the Senate, said on 16 November that he is the underdog but is gaining ground. Democrats won control of the Senate in the midterms, so their leader is set to become majority leader. Senate Democrats choose in a secret ballot in early December.
stories.why_it_matters: The majority leader decides which bills the Senate takes up, so the vote shapes what Congress does for the next two years.

key_facts.fact: Senator Chris Van Hollen, speaking on NPR's Morning Edition on Monday 16 November, said he can beat Chuck Schumer: 'I'm the underdog, but we are really moving in the right direction here.'
Van Hollen said he will run for Senate majority leader in the next Congress, challenging Democratic leader Chuck Schumer after the party swept to power in the midterm elections.
Van Hollen announced his challenge on Thursday 12 November.
Van Hollen will need close to 30 votes, a simple majority of the Senate Democratic caucus, to win.
The vote will be decided by secret ballot behind closed doors, so it is hard to know how many votes each candidate has.
Axios puts the leadership vote on 1 December.
Schumer said: 'I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader.'
Axios reports Schumer has public support from 14 senators, including himself, compared with five for Van Hollen.
Van Hollen framed his bid as a call for change, saying 'we need new leadership.'

stories.geography: Washington, DC; Maryland; New York

stories.headline: Modi in Manila for ASEAN-India and East Asia Summits, With a Quad Meeting Alongside
stories.what_happened: Prime Minister Narendra Modi arrived in Manila on 16 November for a two-day visit to attend the 23rd ASEAN-India Summit and the 21st East Asia Summit on 17 November. He is also expected at the first in-person Quad leaders' meeting in two years, with the leaders of the US, Japan and Australia, and will mark the start of redevelopment at Manila's oldest Sikh gurdwara.
stories.why_it_matters: India calls ASEAN a central pillar of its Act East Policy; the summits cover trade, sea security and stability in the Indo-Pacific.

key_facts.fact: PM Narendra Modi arrived in Manila on Monday 16 November 2026 for a two-day visit.
He is attending the 23rd ASEAN-India Summit and the 21st East Asia Summit, at the invitation of Philippine President Ferdinand R. Marcos Jr.; the summits are on 17 November.
The Philippines is hosting as ASEAN Chair for 2026.
According to the Ministry of External Affairs, the ASEAN-India Summit will review progress on the Comprehensive Strategic Partnership, including the ASEAN-India Plan of Action 2026-2030.
India and ASEAN are marking 2026 as the ASEAN-India Year of Maritime Cooperation; 2027 will mark 35 years of Dialogue Relations.
The MEA called India-ASEAN relations 'a central pillar of India's Act East Policy and our vision for the Indo-Pacific.'
Modi said ASEAN ties are rooted in centuries of civilisational exchanges and span trade, connectivity, maritime security, technology and people-to-people relations.
Modi described the East Asia Summit as an 'important platform for dialogue on regional and global challenges.'
India is focused on the ongoing review of the ASEAN-India Trade in Goods Agreement.
At a community reception Modi watched 'Sita: The Ramayana Revisited', staged by a performing arts group from Iligan City, and a Filipino Ramayana adaptation, 'Maharadia Lawana', was also performed.
At a gala dinner hosted by Marcos at the Philippine International Convention Centre on Monday evening, Modi wore a Barong Tagalog, the Philippine formal shirt.

On Tuesday Modi will take part in a ceremony marking the start of redevelopment at Gurudwara Khalsa Diwan in Manila, established in 1929 by Punjabi migrants and the oldest Sikh place of worship in the Philippines.

The Quad leaders' meeting in Manila is expected to bring together Modi, US President Donald Trump, Japanese PM Sanae Takaichi and Australian PM Anthony Albanese; it is the group's first leaders-level meeting since September 2024.
The Philippines' chairmanship has focused attention on maritime security and ASEAN-China talks on a South China Sea Code of Conduct.

Fuel and power prices were 32.84% higher than a year earlier, while wholesale food inflation eased slightly to 8.58%.

key_facts.fact: WPI-based inflation rose to 12.29% in October 2026, up from 11.39% in September, according to government data released on Monday 16 November.
The rise came from higher costs of fuel and power, primary articles and manufactured goods.
The WPI for all commodities was 113.3 in October, compared with 112.5 in September; this is preliminary data from the Ministry of Commerce and Industry.
Fuel and power inflation rose to 32.84% from 25.85%.
Mineral oils inflation was 45.57%, and electricity inflation moved to 8.06% from a 0.43% fall in September.
Primary articles inflation rose to 9.24% from 8.67%; manufactured goods inflation eased to 9.54% from 9.76%.

ICRA's Rahul Agrawal said the print beat ICRA's 11.8% estimate and that 'fuel and power accounted for 83 basis points' of the 90 basis-point rise.
Bank of Baroda chief economist Madan Sabnavis said the increases will 'pressurise companies into increasing their product prices'; firms have passed on only a limited part so far.
Sabnavis put the fuel surge down to a low base, higher crude oil prices and strong power demand during heat waves in several states.

stories.headline: RTI Reply: Power Lines, Trains, Poaching and Poison Killed Over 1,760 Elephants Since 2009
stories.what_happened: A reply from the Union environment ministry to a Right to Information request, reported on 16 November, says more than 1,760 elephants died from electrocution, train collisions, poaching and poisoning between 2009-10 and 2025-26. Electrocution caused two out of three of these deaths.
stories.why_it_matters: Most of these deaths come from human-made dangers along elephants' paths, which campaigners say can be prevented.

key_facts.fact: More than 1,760 elephants died in India from electrocution, train collisions, poaching and poisoning between 2009-2010 and 2025-2026, according to the Union environment ministry's reply to an RTI query.
Electrocution caused 1,185 deaths (67%), train collisions 277 (16%), poaching 222 (13%) and poisoning 81 (5%).
Between 2021-2022 and 2025-2026 there were 441 electrocution deaths, a 65% increase on the first period reported.
Odisha recorded the most electrocution deaths (238), followed by Karnataka (195) and Assam (191).
Over the whole period Assam recorded the most train-collision deaths (90), followed by West Bengal (68).
For all causes combined, Odisha had 371 deaths, Assam 356 and Karnataka 223.
RTI activist Amit Gupta, who filed the query, said: 'Electrocution is not an accident.'

Gupta blamed illegal electric fences, sagging wires and uninsulated power lines in elephant corridors, and said train deaths come from failures to slow trains, build underpasses and protect corridors.

Background (October 2025): India's first DNA-based count of wild elephants (SAIEE 2021-25), by the Environment Ministry, Project Elephant and the Wildlife Institute of India, estimated 22,446 wild elephants (range 18,255 to 26,645), compared with 27,312 in the 2017 count.
Background (October 2025): scientists collected 21,056 dung samples and used DNA fingerprinting to identify individual elephants; Karnataka has the most elephants (6,013), ahead of Assam (4,159).

Background (2023): a report by the environment ministry's Project Elephant, with state forest departments and the Wildlife Institute of India, identified 150 elephant corridors across 15 states; West Bengal has the most.

stories.headline: India Beat Pakistan Off the Last Ball to Win the Under-19 Asia Cup
stories.what_happened: In the Under-19 Asia Cup final in Al Amerat, Oman, on Saturday 14 November, India chased Pakistan's 337 for 9 and won by one wicket when Mohit Ulva hit the final ball for four. India had been 252 for 8 before a 57-run stand between Manal Chauhan and Ulva.
stories.why_it_matters: It is India's ninth Under-19 Asia Cup title, won against the defending champions.

key_facts.fact: India beat Pakistan by one wicket in the Under-19 Asia Cup final in Al Amerat, Oman, on Saturday 14 November, with the winning runs off the final ball.
Pakistan were the defending champions.
Pakistan made 337 for 9: Usman Khan 107 off 106 balls, Abdul Qadir 80 off 54 balls and Farhan Yousaf 60; Kavya Patel took 4 for 68.
India made 339 for 9 in 50 overs: Lakshya Raichandani 80, Aaryavir Sehwag 58, Manal Chauhan 47 and Mohit Ulva 49 not out.
Raichandani and Sehwag added 95 for the first wicket.
India were 252 for 8 in the 42nd over, and Pakistan seemed close to victory.
Manal Chauhan (47 off 32 balls) and Mohit Ulva (49 not out off 26 balls) put on 57 runs for the ninth wicket.
India needed 8 runs from the final over, then 3 from the final ball; Ulva hit leg-spinner Ahmed Hussain wide of long-off for four.
Number 11 batter C Venkata was 11 not out at the other end.
It was India's ninth Under-19 Asia Cup title.

stories.what_happened: Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland, who is challenging Chuck Schumer to lead the Democrats in the Senate, said on 16 November that he is the underdog but is gaining ground. Democrats won control of the Senate in the midterms, so their leader is set to become majority leader. Senate Democrats choose in a secret ballot in early December.
stories.why_it_matters: The majority leader decides which bills the Senate takes up, so the vote shapes what Congress does for the next two years.

Van Hollen said he will run for Senate majority leader in the next Congress, challenging Democratic leader Chuck Schumer after the party swept to power in the midterm elections.
Van Hollen announced his challenge on Thursday 12 November.
Van Hollen will need close to 30 votes, a simple majority of the Senate Democratic caucus, to win.
The vote will be decided by secret ballot behind closed doors, so it is hard to know how many votes each candidate has.
Axios puts the leadership vote on 1 December.
Schumer said: 'I have the votes to continue serving as Democratic Leader.'
Axios reports Schumer has public support from 14 senators, including himself, compared with five for Van Hollen.
Van Hollen framed his bid as a call for change, saying 'we need new leadership.'

stories.headline: Burnham Says 'The Brexit We Were Given Has Not Worked' Ahead of Friday's UK-EU Summit
stories.what_happened: Prime Minister Andy Burnham was due to say in a speech on 16 November at the Lord Mayor's Banquet in London that leaving the EU has cost Britain more than it gained. On Friday 20 November he goes to Brussels for his first formal UK-EU summit, where he is expected to sign deals on food, energy and a youth scheme letting young people study and work in each other's countries. The Conservatives accuse Labour of taking Britain back into the EU 'via the back door'.
stories.why_it_matters: The deals would change how easily British businesses trade with Europe and whether young Britons can study and work in EU countries.

key_facts.fact: Labour Prime Minister Andy Burnham was expected to say in a speech on Monday 16 November that leaving the EU had cost Britain more than it benefited it.
He was expected to say: 'The Brexit we were given has not worked. We have lost more than we have gained.'
He argues the promise to 'take back control' was not fulfilled, and that a 'needlessly hard' departure created barriers for businesses trading with EU countries.
The speech was to be given at the Lord Mayor's Banquet in the City of London, ahead of an EU summit in Brussels on Friday.
At the summit Burnham is expected to sign deals on food and energy and a scheme that would let young EU citizens study and work in the UK, and young Britons in the EU.
Burnham claims the agreements could add about $22.5 billion to the economy, roughly 0.4% of GDP, and called them 'a win-win.'

Burnham said he would sign an agreement only if it matches Labour's 2024 manifesto and red lines, improves on the existing Brexit deal, better reflects what voters believed they were getting in the 2016 referendum, and brings visible benefits to ordinary people.
No major changes would be agreed before the next election, due by August 2029 at the latest.
The Conservative Party accused Labour of 'dragging us into the European Union via the back door', arguing Britain would have to follow EU rules without a say in shaping them.
The 20 November summit in Brussels is Burnham's first formal UK-EU summit.
52% of voters backed Leave in the referendum.
The EU objects to the UK's demand for an annual cap on the youth scheme, and wants EU students in the UK to pay the lower 'home' university fees.
The UK has agreed to rejoin the Erasmus student exchange programme in 2027.
Talks are expected to largely conclude on food and drink, emissions trading and youth mobility; talks have run for eighteen months.
Burnham addressed European leaders at a European Political Community meeting in Dublin the previous Thursday, alongside Ukraine's President Zelenskyy.

stories.headline: After a Faulty Router Grounded US Flights, Air Travel Returns to Normal
stories.what_happened: On Friday 13 November the FAA stopped all departing flights across the US for more than four hours after its communications network became unstable. Officials traced the problem to a router being replaced at a remote facility in El Dorado, Arkansas, which flooded older equipment with data. By Monday 16 November flights were close to normal, and the government is asking Congress for more money to modernise the system.
stories.why_it_matters: Air traffic control relies on an aging network; the outage stranded thousands of travellers and shows why the system is being upgraded.

key_facts.fact: The FAA ordered a nationwide ground stop at 3:36 p.m. ET on Friday 13 November, while about 3,500 flights were in the air; all of those planes landed safely.
The ground stop was lifted around 8:20 p.m. ET Friday and lasted more than four hours.
It was the first nationwide ground stop since January 2023, when an FAA computer system malfunctioned; the one before followed the 11 September 2001 attacks.
On Friday about 9,159 flights were cancelled and 7,190 delayed, according to FlightAware.
FAA chief Bryan Bedford said 50,000 flights were scheduled Friday and 30,000 had been completed when the stop began.

On Sunday more than 2,300 US flights were cancelled and more than 10,400 delayed, though not all delays came from the ground stop; by 6:30 a.m. ET Monday about 250 Monday flights had been cancelled and 850 delayed.
Operations were slowly returning to normal or close to it at most major airlines on Monday 16 November.
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a contractor from L3Harris, working at a remote FAA site, was switching old copper wire to fiber and replacing a router.
The new router began flooding other routers and overloaded the system, with about 1,000 log-on attempts every four to five seconds.
The FAA traced the problem to a router upgrade at a radio facility in El Dorado, Arkansas; a similar upgrade at a radar facility in Amarillo, Texas, weeks earlier compounded it.
Communications disruptions hit 17 of the FAA's 22 Air Route Traffic Control Centers.

L3Harris, a defence contractor, owns and operates the telecommunications network that connects America's air traffic control system; the network is linked by thousands of aging industrial routers being replaced with new models.
Bedford said about 70% of the system has been moved from copper to fiber, and that the ground stop was issued 'out of an abundance of caution.'
Officials said there was no sign of a cyberattack; Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there were no indications of one.

Duffy said the FAA's modernisation is funded by a $12.5 billion down payment, which he said is not enough; the Trump administration raised its air traffic control funding request to $30 billion late Friday.
Two members of Congress, Rick Larsen and Andre Carson, said only $1 billion of the $12.5 billion approved by Congress has been used.
Officials said it is safe to fly; Duffy advised travellers to check with their airlines before going to the airport.

stories.headline: Euclid Space Telescope Finds Its First Comet, Between Jupiter and Saturn
stories.what_happened: The European Space Agency's Euclid telescope, built to map dark matter and dark energy, has found its first comet, C/2026 S1, about 1.3 billion km away between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn. A University of Helsinki scientist's software spotted a streak across several images, and a fuzzy cloud around the object showed it was an active comet.
stories.why_it_matters: It shows a telescope designed for distant galaxies can also find objects in our own solar system.

key_facts.fact: The European Space Agency's Euclid space telescope discovered its first comet, designated C/2026 S1, or 'comet Euclid' for short.
Euclid is an ESA mission launched in 2023, with contributions from NASA.
The comet was about 807 million miles (1.3 billion km) away when observed, between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.
The observations were captured between 16 and 24 September.
Mikko Pontinen, a scientist at the University of Helsinki, made the discovery with the Solar System Objects Science Working Group of the Euclid Consortium.
Pontinen's software flagged 'a streak' smeared across several images, the sign of a fast-moving object.
He predicted where it would be to find it in other images, eventually locating it in five sets of images.
A closer look showed a fuzzy cloud around the object, which shows an active object, such as a comet, shedding dust and gas.
The team checked existing comet records to confirm it was new.
Euclid was designed for long, slow observations of distant galaxies to help scientists study dark energy and dark matter, not to image fast-moving comets.
Future scientists might aim Euclid at comets in the outer solar system on purpose, and such finds help researchers spot 'noise' like comet trails in Euclid's images.
Background: Euclid lifted off on a SpaceX Falcon 9 rocket from Cape Canaveral, Florida, on 1 July 2023, to survey one third of the sky over six years.
Background: Euclid observes from the Sun-Earth Lagrange point 2 (L2), on average 1.5 million km from Earth; its nominal survey started on 14 February 2024.

stories.headline: A Cosmic Magnifying Glass Could Show the Same Exploding Star Twice More, in About 70 Years
stories.what_happened: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope found SN Ares, a supernova whose light was bent and magnified by a massive galaxy cluster. Lens models predict two more images of the same explosion will arrive in about 73 and 76 years, because the light took longer paths around the cluster.
stories.why_it_matters: Timing the delayed images could give one of the most precise single measurements of how fast the universe is expanding.

key_facts.fact: Astronomers found SN Ares, an exploding star (supernova), in James Webb Space Telescope near-infrared images of the galaxy cluster MACS J0308.9+2645, first spotted in August 2025.
The supernova happened about 8.8 billion years ago.
The lead author is Conor Larison of the Space Telescope Science Institute.
A massive galaxy cluster between Earth and a distant galaxy acts as a natural lens, bending and magnifying the background galaxy's light; this is called gravitational lensing.
Lensing can create several images of the same galaxy; light taking slightly different paths arrives at different times, sometimes hours and sometimes decades apart.
Only one magnified image of SN Ares has been seen so far; three lens models predict two more images will arrive in about 73 and 76 years.
The team says the system has 'by far the highest predicted delays of any discovered lensed SN system so far.'
JWST spectroscopy showed helium and hydrogen, making it a Type IIb supernova, a star that lost most of its outer hydrogen layer before exploding.
Measuring the gap between arrival times could pin down the Hubble constant, the universe's expansion rate, and could be one of the most precise single estimates of it.
The team plans more measurements in early 2027 to refine its predictions.
Phys.org published the report on 14 November 2026; the discovery paper was posted to arXiv on 23 October.
SN Ares was found by VENUS, a James Webb Space Telescope survey of galaxy clusters; it is the first lensed supernova found by the VENUS program.
The closer the light passes to the centre of the galaxy cluster, the larger the delay caused by gravitational time dilation, so images nearest the cluster centre arrive last.

Background: measurements of the universe's expansion rate disagree, about 67 km/s/Mpc from the cosmic microwave background versus about 73 km/s/Mpc from the distance ladder, a puzzle known as the Hubble tension; lensed-supernova time delays offer an independent way to measure it.

stories.what_happened: England beat world champions Spain 3-2 in a UEFA Nations League match in Madrid on Sunday 15 November, ending Spain's 43-match unbeaten run and taking top spot in their group. Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White scored, and goalkeeper James Trafford made late saves after England went down to ten men.
stories.why_it_matters: The win sends England top of their Nations League group.

key_facts.fact: England beat Spain 3-2 in Madrid on Sunday 15 November 2026 in the UEFA Nations League, ending the world champions' 43-match unbeaten run.
Harry Kane scored a first-half penalty, and Ezri Konsa's header and Ben White's finish came within five second-half minutes.
England were reduced to ten men after Elliot Anderson brought down Lamine Yamal, and Mikel Oyarzabal scored the penalty for Spain.
Goalkeeper James Trafford started ahead of Jordan Pickford and made late saves as England held on.
England's win took them to the top of their Nations League group, ahead of Spain on goal difference.

stories.headline: Estonia Will Close Its Border Crossings With Russia After a Foiled Attack on a Drone Factory
stories.what_happened: Estonia says it will close all its border crossings with Russia from 1 December after stopping what it calls an arson attempt ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence on a drone factory near Tallinn. Eight people living in Latvia were arrested. Russia says it will check whether the plan is real and called it Russophobia.
stories.why_it_matters: The crossings are among the few overland links between Russia and the EU still open, and European countries say Russia's 'hybrid' attacks are spreading beyond Ukraine.

key_facts.fact: Estonia said on Sunday 15 November it would close its border with Russia after stopping what it called an attempted arson attack on a drone factory ordered by Russia's GRU military intelligence.
Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna wrote: 'Estonia will close all Estonian-Russian border crossing points as of 1 December.'
The target was Threod Systems, an Estonian defence company in Viimsi, north of Tallinn, which makes reconnaissance and attack drones.
Prime Minister Kristen Michal said the GRU ordered a 'sabotage attempt' on Saturday night; heightened security and a quick police response averted extensive damage and the attackers were detained.
Chief prosecutor Astrid Asi said security forces arrested eight people living in Latvia.
Michal described the incident as part of Russia's wider 'hybrid war' against Europe and said Estonia 'will not be intimidated.'
Russian foreign ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova said Moscow would check whether Estonia planned to shut all crossings and, if so, would see it as more aggressive Russophobia.
In August, Milrem Robotics, a defence subcontractor in Tallinn, was targeted in an attempted arson attack, and Latvian nationals were arrested.
Estonia, an EU and NATO member, has three crossings with Russia: Narva in the north, and Luhamaa and Koidula in the south.
Russia suspended vehicle traffic through Narva in February 2024, but people on foot can still cross.
These crossings are among the few overland links between Russia and the EU still operating since Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022.
Tsahkna said he had told the Finnish, Latvian and Lithuanian foreign ministers about the decision.
Romania said drones struck three ships near the Sulina Canal, which links the Danube to the Black Sea, on Sunday 15 November; no one was hurt and crews put out fires.
Romania's Foreign Minister Dan Neculaescu said: 'We have had four alerts in 24 hours, and we have had three ships hit over the weekend. This is unacceptable.'
Sweden's Foreign Minister Maria Malmer Stenergard said increased hybrid warfare reflects the Kremlin's frustration that it is not winning in Ukraine; Sweden has spent much more on civil defence.

stories.headline: EU Sanctions Nearly 50 Russian Banks, Approves Its Largest Payment to Ukraine and Says a Ceasefire Must Come First
stories.what_happened: On 16 November EU foreign ministers in Brussels added 113 new names to their sanctions on Russia, including nearly 50 banks and financial institutions, and EU ministers approved a payment of nearly 8 billion euros to Ukraine, the largest single payment under the Ukraine Facility. EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas accused Russia of making demands to keep the war going and said a ceasefire must come first.
stories.why_it_matters: Sanctions and money are Europe's main tools in the war; the EU wants a say in peace talks led by the US and is using them as leverage.

key_facts.fact: EU foreign ministers met in Brussels on Monday 16 November at the Foreign Affairs Council, chaired by EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas.
The new sanctions list 12 individuals and 101 entities, 113 in total, including nearly 50 Russian banks and financial institutions.
The EU Council said: 'The EU is cutting off the financial channels that process state revenues and fund Russia's war effort.'

Also listed are the sole shareholder of Russian online retailer Wildberries, a majority owner of Ozon, companies running Russian refineries and the St Petersburg oil terminal, and firms in the UAE, China, Seychelles and Oman that buy Russian oil products.
People and companies on the list have their assets frozen; EU operators may not give them money or economic resources; the 12 individuals also face EU travel bans.
Dozens of people accused of spreading pro-Russian propaganda and disinformation were also hit with travel bans and asset freezes.
Kallas said Russia was repeating demands made before its full-scale invasion and adding conditions, calling this 'a clear pretext for keeping the war going.'
Kallas wrote on X: 'In 2021, Russia's demands were a pretext for war. In 2026, they are pretext to keep the war going.'
Kallas wrote that 'A ceasefire must come first.'
Kallas said: 'We have leverage. That is our sanctions. That is frozen assets.'
The EU approved a payment of nearly 8 billion euros (about $8.7bn) to Ukraine, its largest-ever single payment under the Ukraine Facility.
Around 5 billion euros of the payment comes from 2026 resources of the Ukraine Support Loan, and the Council says Kyiv completed more than 20 reform steps to unlock it.
The Ukraine Facility dates from March 2024 and offers more than 50 billion euros in grants and loans through 2027; once these funds arrive, total payments since mid-2024 will pass 40 billion euros.
Kyiv also received $1.88bn from the European Commission to buy drones, ammunition and air defence systems, part of a $99bn loan approved in February.
Two days of US-mediated Russia-Ukraine talks in the UAE produced a prisoner exchange but no breakthrough on ending the war.
After the Abu Dhabi talks, the US encouraged Ukraine and its backers to accept a Russian demand for a new European security framework; Europeans see this as an attempt to weaken NATO.

Five countries - the UK, France, Germany, Italy and Poland - plus officials from the European Council and NATO will speak on Europe's behalf in any future peace talks, leaders agreed after a meeting in Dublin.
Russian attacks killed at least three people in Ukraine on Monday, in the Kherson, Dnipropetrovsk and Zaporizhia regions.
Russia's Defence Ministry said it intercepted 1,336 Ukrainian drones overnight.
EU humanitarian chief Hadja Lahbib said Russia is 'turning winter into a weapon of war' as she unveiled a new aid package for Ukraine.
The EU is pushing for a ceasefire followed by a lasting peace agreement; the war is in its fifth year.

stories.headline: Ten-Man England Win 3-2 in Madrid to End Spain's 43-Match Unbeaten Run
stories.what_happened: England beat world champions Spain 3-2 in a UEFA Nations League match in Madrid on Sunday 15 November, ending Spain's 43-match unbeaten run and taking top spot in their group. Harry Kane, Ezri Konsa and Ben White scored, and goalkeeper James Trafford made late saves after England went down to ten men.
stories.why_it_matters: The win sends England top of their Nations League group.

key_facts.fact: England beat Spain 3-2 in Madrid on Sunday 15 November 2026 in the UEFA Nations League, ending the world champions' 43-match unbeaten run.
Harry Kane scored a first-half penalty, and Ezri Konsa's header and Ben White's finish came within five second-half minutes.
England were reduced to ten men after Elliot Anderson brought down Lamine Yamal, and Mikel Oyarzabal scored the penalty for Spain.
Goalkeeper James Trafford started ahead of Jordan Pickford and made late saves as England held on.
England's win took them to the top of their Nations League group, ahead of Spain on goal difference.
The Analyst says Spain's run was the longest ever by a European men's team, and that it was Spain's first international defeat in Madrid for 39 years.
Thomas Tuchel is England's manager.
